    AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • According to recent reports, we will never sell your address.
    • We have sent a confirmation link to .
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    According to recent reports, we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    Sources indicate that as it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    In a recent development, the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries mentioned they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    According to recent reports, despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) noted they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more promptly.

    Recent findings suggest that “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    According to recent reports, using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    It has been revealed that at the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    In a recent development, this also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also demonstrates that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    According to recent reports, the differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a newly introduced dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily owners and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    It has been revealed that A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    It has been revealed that as pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and newly introduced hybrid work schedules.

    On Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff noted “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a tech giant is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.
    • Benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase.
    • Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff noted “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a tech giant is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.

    Benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication.

    Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.

    Salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) says SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for new businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ.

    According to recent reports, contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, said that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.”.

    Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.”.

    Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.”.

    Pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.”.

    Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.”.

    When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.”.

    In terms of making the case for newly introduced businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your plans right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata.

    According to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide states you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI.

    “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • The latest budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    The latest budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    Sources indicate that A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    Industry observers note that that changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    In a recent development, “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan mentioned. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    According to recent reports, RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s major local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a fresh tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    According to recent reports, the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan stated.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Sources indicate that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    Sources indicate that the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Rolled out in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results indicated the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    According to recent reports, “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Industry observers note that many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

    According to recent reports, some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan stated.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    Sources indicate that “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, new data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.
    • Recent findings suggest that wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API.
    • WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, new data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API. Google also published the referrer values its traffic sends and shared ways in which a CDN move could lead to blocking Googlebot. Ask Maps began contacting local businesses, and United Airlines included its AI agent rules within its terms.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    WordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec. 8, contains a upcoming feature called /random/, turned on by default, to send a visitor to a randomly selected published post. There is no option in the dashboard settings for this to be turned off.

    According to recent reports, key facts: According to the developer note, /random/ randomly selects posts and also custom post types as long as they are publicly queryable and have archives (unless the developer has registered them using 'randomable' => false) and excludes pages and attachments. The development code uses a 302 status code along with an X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow HTTP header when it redirects the visitor but does not send that header on the post that the visitor arrives at. To turn the feature off, developers need the wp_enable_random_content_redirect filter, and the different spelling given in WordPress’s November developer news roundup isn’t found anywhere in the code.

    Testimonials for clients (and other custom post type entries) may never be accessed via navigation. When their post type is eligible, they can be reached through /random/, even if they have been set to noindex by an SEO plugin. Before you enhancement, check which post types would meet WordPress’s eligibility criteria, and ask a developer to exclude those that should not show up.

    Recent findings suggest that read our full coverage: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made.

    Teams using the Search Console API can now segment the data they pull into branded and non-branded searches without having to maintain a list of their brands as regular expressions (regex).

    Key facts: Three Performance report features were added to the Search Analytics API by Google on Nov. 16. The brandedClassification dimension works only with eligible properties, and according to the API reference, the data provided for this dimension starts on Feb. 21, 2026. Setting type to webMultimodal returns results from Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android and image uploads, and a new filterLists field allows you to filter by multiple countries or devices in a single request.

    Industry observers note that for reports covering dates before Feb. 21, 2026, you’ll still need your own brand regex. Google’s announcement of the branded queries filter says “some queries may occasionally be misidentified,” so comparing the API split with the regex you already use can help you spot where they differ.

    Read our full coverage: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    A google.com referrer lets you know in your analytics when Google sends a visitor, but it doesn’t show which source (Search, Discover or Google Images) was behind it, notes a new Search Central page.

    Key facts: The page was listed Nov. 12 in Google’s documentation updates log. It indicates Google Search utilizes an origin referrer policy for its Search results; thus, the header will contain only the scheme and host, and not the search query. Referrers from Discover carry the values of the surface where Discover was viewed. Same-origin services such as Google Images send the same values as Search and Discover.

    To distinguish Discover clicks from Search clicks, use Search Console’s Discover report rather than referrer data. If Google traffic appears as referral or direct in your analytics, Google’s page recommends checking whether custom channel rules, referral exclusions, or filters are reclassifying it.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Find Search Traffic In Analytics & Logs.

    A CDN can let Googlebot crawl your site faster before the CDN’s cache has filled, according to Google, and those requests then go to your origin server.

    It has been revealed that key facts: On Nov. 11, Search Central posted Google’s explanation that a fast and reliable CDN may slowly increase a site’s crawl capacity limit, while a brand new CDN begins with an empty cache. The first visit to each URL is a cache miss, so the page has to come from your origin server, and crawlers visit far more of your site’s URLs than visitors do, with most visitors sticking to a small set of popular pages. When admins block all bots from their site using blanket bot protection, they can cause Googlebot to fail CAPTCHA challenges. If this stays in place, then the pages of the site begin to drop out of search results.

    Google’s advice for the move is to allow verified bots in the CDN and firewall settings, then pre-warm caches by fetching your most popular and frequently crawled URLs before switching traffic. Before enabling bot protection during the migration, be sure the verified-bot setting is turned on.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems.

    It has been revealed that google’s Ask Maps has started calling some U.S. beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses to identify available appointment times for customers.

    It has been revealed that key facts: On Nov. 16 a post from Google said that customers can use Ask Maps to find these appointments online and have it call local businesses, then see available time slots so the customer can decide where to book. The feature started rolling out on Android and iOS, with the ability to find appointments launching in the U.S. first. Google already makes automated calls to businesses for customers using Google Search and Maps, including booking appointments and confirming availability, and this process is covered in Google’s Business Profile help page.

    In Google’s demo, Ask Maps shows four times for a gel manicure that it confirmed were available online.

    Industry observers note that the setting Google documents for those automated calls is the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” option in Advanced settings in your verified Business Profile. However, Google’s Ask Maps post does not indicate if calls received via Ask Maps are subject to this setting. Check what you have set, and make sure whoever answers the phone knows these calls come from Google on behalf of a customer.

    Read our full coverage: Google Adds Appointment Finding & Business Calls To Ask Maps.

    Recent findings suggest that united Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, let search engines index its public pages but require written permission for any AI agent that searches, books or buys on its site or app.

    Key facts: The terms also bar using data from United’s site or app, such as fares and schedules, to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt named no AI crawlers or agents. Separately, HUMAN Security’s October report found that Meta’s and OpenAI’s agents made about 90% of the agent requests on sites and apps it protects.

    It has been revealed that in HUMAN Security’s October data, Muse accounted for 59% of agent requests. Three OpenAI agents accounted for about 30% combined.

    It has been revealed that meta’s Muse publishes no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Slobodan Manic wrote in October, so whether it gets in comes down to your terms and bot protection. Muse sent the most requests in HUMAN’s data, and bot rules can check the signatures some of its requests carry, whose key directory DataDome reported had moved to muse.ai by Nov. 9.

    Read our full coverage: United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First and Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data.

    Sources indicate that much of this week’s SEO work sits with teams outside of SEO. The next steps for this week include identifying who is responsible for the off switch for the /random/ redirect, as well as reporting on the branded split and the analytics rules for referrers. Google’s CDN advice should be reviewed by whoever runs the CDN and firewall, and the automated calls toggle is managed through the Business Profile. United’s rules related to agents are contained within a legal agreement. Before the next change, the first step is to determine who has responsibility for each of these in your own organization.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    Sources indicate that for a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    Industry observers note that at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association noted on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    LION Publishers remarked in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson stated.

    OpenNews noted in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism stated Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Industry observers note that journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he remarked. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    • In a recent development, so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    It has been revealed that atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    In a recent development, so far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each day, thousands of people seek our help getting disability benefits or insurance compensation. They’re intimidated by the process, unsure where to turn, and desperate for good advice.

    As a Legal Assistant at Atticus, your job is to ensure they get and stay on the right path. This job is different from that of a traditional legal assistant. The job mixes responsibilities in any good legal assistant’s comfort zone (build client relationships; support paralegals and attorneys in filing and managing claims) with those unique to being an operator in a fast-growing tech tech giant (help Marketing source clients who’d be great in testimonials, or user test upcoming tools for Product).

    In a typical week you might do any of the following:.

    Make contact with a client that’s in danger of slipping through the cracks at SSA, and help get their case back on track.

    Work with a client’s team to run down missing paperwork at SSA.

    Take on an inefficient workflow that’s slowing the team down (e.g., processing case updates), scope an improvement, get team buy-in, and execute the improvement.

    This role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup and do meaningful social impact work. It’s designed to be a path to building expertise in the fields of law you support and taking on greater responsibilities over time (e.g. becoming a paralegal).

    You have a Bachelor’s degree from a four-year university with strong academic performance.

    You have experience in a professional role that required a substantial amount of customer-facing work and/or administrative tasks.

    You are a resourceful team-player ready to dive into a scrappy startup environment where you will learn quickly and get your hands dirty.

    You are comfortable in a variety of interpersonal conversations; you can be empathetic and kind when speaking with people in a moment of crisis, and can be thoughtful and organized when interacting with attorneys or the SSA.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You have professional experience helping others apply for government benefits.

    You have experience at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment.

    We are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you’re from a background that’s underrepresented in tech, we’d love to meet you.

    This is a rare opportunity to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our culture.

    We’re a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity for every employee — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at the end-of-year).

    $1,000/year reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    Industry observers note that we anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $50,000 and $75,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate’s experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    Recent findings suggest that this job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the company dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

    Sources indicate that any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

    Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

    Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet users. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

    Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

    Latest Update: Check Your Nov. 18 Rank Data Before Blaming The Core Upgrade via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, google search results that reached rank tracker Nozzle dropped to about one-tenth of their usual volume for approximately 10 hours on Nov.
    • It has been revealed that some of the blocked searches ended up on a Google page asking customers to sign in prior to seeing search engine results.
    • Recent findings suggest that the numbers reported by Nozzle are based on its own collection through the five SERP data providers which processed the requests made by Nozzle that day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, google search results that reached rank tracker Nozzle dropped to about one-tenth of their usual volume for approximately 10 hours on Nov. 18 based on information from Nozzle. Also during this time frame, Google was still rolling out its November core update.

    It has been revealed that some of the blocked searches ended up on a Google page asking customers to sign in prior to seeing search engine results. On Nov. 17, Rajan Patel, the VP of Engineering for Search at Google, commented that he did not believe this login page was supposed to appear on the first page of search results, though Google could be conducting a test.

    Recent findings suggest that the numbers reported by Nozzle are based on its own collection through the five SERP data providers which processed the requests made by Nozzle that day. So Nozzle’s reports cannot provide evidence of whether other rank tracker companies experienced the same drop in deliveries. Nozzle is a company that sells tools for tracking rankings.

    Recent findings suggest that deliveries to Nozzle fell at all five providers for several hours, as Derek Perkins wrote in an article dated Nov. 18 on the Nozzle blog. Nozzle was collecting normally on Nov. 17 and until late morning UTC on Nov. 18, when deliveries slowed down.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. ET, Nozzle received 11.6% of what would be collected during 10 regular hours. During each provider’s worst hour, that provider received 2% or less of its regular hourly amount.

    Nozzle’s hourly chart shows when the drop began and when deliveries started to recover.

    One of the providers also told Nozzle that there had been an increase in CAPTCHAs on its iPhone searches, going up from approximately 19% of total requests to approximately 90%. Thirty-one percent of a sample of blocked attempts from that provider ended up on Google’s sign-in page and the remainder on a CAPTCHA. Searches made from desktop computers were hardly affected, Nozzle notes.

    The sign-in page shows “Sign in to continue” with the line “Sign in to verify you’re a human and see more results.” The sign-in button does not link to the search results, according to Nozzle.

    Here’s what the prompt looked like in Clark’s incognito window.

    Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 16, Brodie Clark, who runs SERPalerts, posted a video from an incognito window showing that prior to seeing any results, the user had to enter their credentials.

    The following day, Patel responded to Clark’s post.

    Looking into this. I don’t believe it’s meant to happen on the first page of results like this but we may be testing something here….

    Nozzle’s requests also encountered CAPTCHAs and a delay page. From Perkins’s perspective, a CAPTCHA can be solved and the delay waited out, but neither option works on the sign-in wall.

    According to recent reports, the wall adds to the goto link limits I covered on Nov. 5, which cap how fast tools can follow the result links on one Google results page.

    Industry observers note that the time period of Nozzle’s 10-hour fall in collection coincided with the time frame during which Google’s November core revision, which started Nov. 10, was still being rolled out. According to Google’s dashboard, the rollout “may take up to 2 weeks to complete” and there were no entries indicating completion when I reviewed the page on Nov. 22.

    Prior to reporting a Nov. 18 ranking drop as part of the core upgrade, first verify whether your rank tracker pulled regular Google search results that day, beginning with mobile. When a drop coincides with a core update, follow Google’s instructions by using Search Console, waiting at least one full week beyond the time when the rollout is finished and then trying a comparison of that week with the week prior to its start.

    Google’s dashboard will show the end date once the core upgrade is complete.

    The sign-in page didn’t go away when Nozzle’s drop ended. It still appeared on a little under 1% of page loads at the provider that reported the iPhone CAPTCHAs, according to Nozzle’s Derek Perkins.

    The Cornell Daily Sun saw traffic spike by almost 500% in September.

    RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026We’ve now been publishing roundups of local newspaper traffic for a full year, so we can compare this year’s traffic to last year’s. Almost across the board, local newspapers are seeing traffic decline as Google referrals drop. For July, August, and September, traffic to the most-visited sites is lower than at this time last year, according to our Similarweb data.

    Sources indicate that RELATED ARTICLEHow did newspapers in places like Harrisburg, Birmingham, and Syracuse become some of America’s most-read online?Joshua BentonJuly 23, 2025A good example is Advance Local’s Harrisburg Patriot-News, PennLive.com. Josh has written about Advance publications punching above their weight in traffic. They still are: Advance outlets like AL.com, Mlive.com, and NJ.com, among others, continued to feature prominently in the top sites by estimated monthly visits in July, August, and September. In August 2026, PennLive’s traffic growth stood out even among Advance peers; it gained 3.6 million visits in August compared to July, a 78% spike. But in total, PennLive saw a little over 8.2 million monthly visits for August 2026 — down from about 12.5 million in August 2025.

    Still, publishers large and small are finding ways to bring more readers to their sites. In August, the Bozeman Daily Chronicle grew its traffic by about 96,000 monthly visits, a 49% jump. Managing editor Jack Reaney attributed the growth to the newspaper launching a latest website Aug. 3 designed for improved functionality, with “fewer, more intentional news categories,” lighter page design for faster load times, and a more modern layout. The Chronicle is one of more than 150 newspapers owned by Adams MultiMedia. The parent organization is rolling out the new website design across its newspapers, but Bozeman was the “guinea pig,” Reaney said.

    Industry observers note that in Florida, Cape Coral Breeze, a small weekly, saw its traffic spike about 139% in August. The network of local weeklies has tried to adopt a daily, real-time mindset after decades of posting once a week, Breeze Newspapers publisher Ray Eckenrode told me. The August spike was driven by participation in Cape Coral Breeze’s “Best of Cape Coral” contest, where readers vote on favorite local businesses in more than 200 categories. According to the team’s internal count, a little over 150,000 “Best of” votes were cast this year, up from 92,000 last year. The team made an effort this year to “drive traffic to our homepage first to reach the contest voting page to expose some of those casual website customers to our news coverage,” Eckenrode stated, and had some success with that strategy.

    In September, The Cornell Daily Sun gained 1 million visits, almost a 500% jump from August, when it broke the story of the Cornell 7 lawsuit (and published an editorial naming the defendants). Other local news sites in Latest York also saw meaningful growth in September; traffic to NNY360.com jumped 84%, while the Gannett-owned Democrat and Chronicle gained about 762,000 visits, a 35% jump.

    On the opposite coast, the San-Jose-based Mercury News gained around 690,000 monthly visits in September, a 14% jump. “Our traffic is volatile like everyone else’s, but we had a strong September mainly because a couple of stories performed very well,” noted Annika Toernqvist, MediaNews Group’s managing editor for digital for Northern California. Environmental beat reporter Paul Rogers‘ story about a latest California law that will ban watering artificial turf “performed exceptionally well on Google and Google Discovery”; 62% of traffic to the story came from search. Stories about the local impact of new state laws consistently do well with the outlet’s readers, according to Toernqvist, and this was “a hot topic with a strong headline.” The story was also the top subscription converter in September. Another story by Rogers covering the proposed renaming of Fremont State Park also drove traffic that month; 86% came from search, mostly from Google Discovery.

    Meanwhile, celebrity reporter Martha Ross‘ story about a newly introduced book on King Charles’ valet performed well in part thanks to a bump from…the Drudge Report. (“Yes, the Drudge Report still drives traffic,” Toernqvist stated; it accounted for 43% of visits to that story.).

    35 AI Prompts & Examples For SEO (Updated November 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting.
    • Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.
    • According to recent reports, apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting. At Search Engine Journal, the team experiments with AI to wrangle data, handle repetitive tasks, and do deep analysis.

    Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.

    According to recent reports, apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data. For analysis and reporting, SEO tools can provide the keyword estimates, backlink records, clicks, impressions, and performance data that an LLM doesn’t have. Connect those to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and, with the right prompts and some prodding, you can ask more complex questions. For example, which pages have conflicting canonicals, serve a valuable product category, and can be fixed without a template rebuild?

    It has been revealed that the following list of 35 prompts covers a range of SEO applications. Many of them need a data connection or an export, and they are designed to take your prompting beyond the basics.

    Use this guide as a basis to experiment, adapt to your own needs and clients, and build your own SEO prompt library.

    Before you copy and run a prompt from this list, read the setup guidance below.

    Recent findings suggest that the tools an AI needs depend on the work. For a copy review, provide the text and your requirements. For analysis, provide the data. For current research or private SEO data, make sure the AI can access the relevant sources.

    After analysis, check that the results cover the intended data and that notable calculations are sound.

    Available tools depend on the account and workspace. So check the current documentation for ChatGPT files, Claude file creation, and Gemini file analysis.

    For connected SEO data, follow the provider’s setup instructions. Check subscription, API allowance, and dataset requirements, and set a retrieval limit when API usage is charged.

    An effective prompt gives an LLM a clear task, useful context, and specific constraints. When you ask it to work with evidence, add the instruction below to whichever prompt you use:.

    Industry observers note that use customer research to identify the tasks and needs behind people’s questions. The prompt turns those needs into potential search queries, while keeping evidence from customers separate from ideas that still need validation.

    In a recent development, you need: Customer research, a seed topic, and a clear picture of your audience. Text analysis is enough to map needs; add a keyword export or SEO connector if you also want demand estimates.

    Sources indicate that use a topic and audience to generate distinct questions that could help readers complete a task. The prompt separates questions found in your data from research hypotheses, then recommends which belong in an existing article, a separate resource, or neither.

    Read more about query fan-out for background on this topic and note that Google’s current AI search guidance cautions against creating pages for every possible query variation.

    An optional source is the Bing AI Performance report. Its sampled grounding queries show retrieval phrases associated with cited content, but they are not necessarily user prompts and do not reveal Google’s fan-out queries.

    According to recent reports, you need: A topic, an audience, and your existing content. Query data can help validate ideas, but you don’t need a specialist connector to generate them.

    Recent findings suggest that check whether an article answers the relevant questions your audience has. The prompt identifies meaningful gaps and proposes only the changes needed to address them, while flagging facts that need research or expert input. Use this template to assess query coverage. If the glitch is how the content explains or presents its information, use the content enhancement prompt instead.

    You need: The article, the reader’s goal, and a list of observed or proposed queries. Include sources for any facts the revision needs.

    Group keywords by search intent and identify which existing or potential page could serve each group. The prompt checks the data before using it and treats overlapping page targets as candidates for review, not proof of cannibalization.

    You need: A keyword export with metric definitions and a page inventory. Upload the export for data analysis, or use an authorized SEO connector to retrieve equivalent data.

    For prompts that need to inspect live webpages, an Exa or Firecrawl integration can help retrieve page content. For Google ranking data, use a SERP API or supported connector, such as Ahrefs, DataForSEO, or SerpApi.

    Automated Google searches can return results that look plausible but differ from those a person sees in a normal search. SEJ’s report on SERP poisoning explains the issue. Some providers offer safeguards to detect or resolve misleading results. These can reduce errors, but they cannot guarantee accurate results.

    Industry observers note that dataForSEO’s resolve_poisoned_results option is off by default. When enabled, it detects and resolves poisoned results and adds the cost of one SERP page to the task.

    It has been revealed that keep the search engine, location, language, and device settings consistent, and record when each result set was collected. To compare ranking changes, use two snapshots collected with matching settings. If you do not have a live connector, use dated SERP exports.

    Compare two ranking snapshots to show which queries and pages moved, appeared, or disappeared. The prompt separates observed changes from possible explanations and identifies what evidence would help explain them.

    You need: Two dated rank-tracker or SERP exports collected with matching settings for search engine, market, device, and ranking convention, plus a log of relevant site changes between the two dates. File analysis is enough to compare them.

    It has been revealed that review the pages ranking for a query to understand the needs, audiences, and decision stages they serve. The prompt uses that evidence to recommend a purpose and format for your page without treating common SERP patterns as proven ranking factors.

    Industry observers note that use this before deciding what a page should do. Choose the content comparison template when you already have a page to audit against the results.

    Industry observers note that you need: A dated SERP sample, accessible result pages, and a brief or draft of your proposed page. The AI needs web access to review the result pages.

    Industry observers note that generate title options that match the page’s search intent and accurately reflect its content. Each option is tied to a reader need and a supporting passage, so you can check that the title’s promise is supported. Use character count as an editing guide, not a fixed Google limit, as Google may shorten displayed titles to fit the available width.

    Recent findings suggest that use this prompt for title alternatives. Choose the metadata review when you need to diagnose existing titles and descriptions and strategy how to evaluate changes.

    According to recent reports, you need: The page content, its target search intent, and your brand rules. No plugin is needed.

    Decide whether a page needs an upgrade, a clearer focus, a separate page, consolidation review, or no change. The prompt checks time-sensitive claims and uses the site inventory, search intent, performance data, and business goal to explain its recommendation.

    According to recent reports, you need: The current page, a site inventory, dated search-performance data, and the business goal. Use web research to check claims that may have changed.

    Industry observers note that review whether the content gives readers enough evidence to assess its claims, authorship, methods, and sources. The prompt identifies what is already supported, what is missing, and what needs to be verified without inventing experience or credentials.

    You need: The content and verified information about its author, organization, methods, and sources.

    In a recent development, build a year-long initiative that connects content ideas to reader needs and business objectives. This prompt checks existing coverage, seasonality, launch dates, and team capacity, while keeping later plans provisional where evidence is limited.

    You need: Keyword or trend data, launch dates, an existing content inventory, and production capacity. Enable file creation to produce a spreadsheet. A calendar connector is optional if you provide the dates.

    According to recent reports, assess whether pages should stay separate, be differentiated, updated, or consolidated. The prompt weighs duplicated information against distinct reader needs and outlines what to preserve if a merge is recommended.

    In a recent development, you need: The candidate pages, crawl and internal-link data, query-to-page performance, and relevant backlink data. Uploaded exports are enough for data analysis.

    In a recent development, review a draft for factual accuracy, sourcing, attribution, contradictions, and clear style challenges. The prompt also flags generic sections that need stronger evidence or examples, without claiming to certify originality or authorship.

    According to recent reports, you need: The draft, your house style, sources, and any material for comparison. Use web access to check missing or current factual references.

    Study a defined sample of competitor pages to understand the topics, formats, and evidence they use. The prompt identifies strategic options based on that sample without assuming it reveals the competitor’s full strategy or performance.

    Use this to study publishing patterns and strategic choices. Choose coverage gaps when you need a prioritized list of unmet reader needs from two content inventories.

    You need: Competitor content inventories, your own content or assets, and a limit on the research. Use browsing or a bounded crawl; performance comparisons require actual data.

    Compare your page with a defined set of ranking pages using a dated SERP export or provider dataset. This prompt looks at reader needs, evidence, examples, and decision support, then identifies where your page can improve or contribute something different.

    You need: The keyword, market, device, a dated SERP export, and your content. An authorized provider connection can supply the export; ordinary web search cannot replace a ranking snapshot.

    Find places where a link would help readers, using only the destinations you supply. Each recommendation includes the existing anchor text and a reason for the link, with questionable or unsuitable URLs flagged for checking.

    It has been revealed that you need: The source article and a current destination list with URLs, summaries, and status. No connector is needed if you provide these.

    Sources indicate that review whether the title and description match the page and its search intent. Suggest alternatives based on the content, then outline how to assess any change using comparable data without assuming it will improve click-through rate.

    You need: The current metadata, page content, a comparable SERP sample, and optional query performance data. Text analysis is enough.

    Identify specific explanations, evidence, or visuals that would make the page more useful. Recommend additions only when they address a reader’s need, and flag any research or assets still required.

    In a recent development, you need: The content, the reader’s task, available assets, and relevant data. Image or chart tools are optional if you want approved additions produced.

    Use screenshots to review the page’s visible layout and messaging, then suggest tests for potential improvements. Keep visual observations separate from hypotheses about behavior, speed, or functionality.

    Industry observers note that you need: Desktop and mobile screenshots, the page content, and the conversion goal. Include funnel or performance data to assess visitor behavior or page speed.

    Assess whether each location has enough distinct customer need and verified information to justify its own page. For locations that qualify, draft relevant copy and flag local details that still need confirmation.

    You need: Confirmed service areas, local business facts, offers, and supporting evidence. Use web research to check current local sources.

    Turn real customer questions into concise answers based on approved business information. Check current local rules against official sources and flag questions that need a business decision or further verification.

    In a recent development, you need: Actual customer questions, approved business information, and current official sources for local rules. No FAQ plugin is needed to draft answers.

    Recent findings suggest that use backlink data to find relevant pages that may have a reason to reference your work. Check the source pages and your assets before drafting specific outreach – the recommendations are not guaranteed placements, and no messages are sent.

    It has been revealed that you need: A backlink gap export or authorized SEO provider connection, your relevant assets, and web research access. Set a maximum number of pages to inspect.

    Compare your content with a competitor’s to find reader needs your pages may not serve. Prioritize possible gaps using business relevance and any demand data you provide, rather than assuming a competitor’s topic proves demand.

    Industry observers note that you need: Your content inventory, a competitor’s inventory, and readable pages. Add keyword or performance data for quantitative prioritization.

    Turn SEO evidence into either an analytical report or a one-page executive memo. Calculate from raw data when needed, explain what the evidence supports, and make ROI claims only when the value and cost basis are agreed.

    You need: Search and analytics exports or checked performance metrics, source definitions, comparable periods, business goals, and a change log. Include costs and an agreed value basis if you want an ROI calculation. Use data analysis for calculations – text analysis is enough to summarize checked findings.

    Compare crawl, sitemap, and URL Inspection evidence to investigate why important pages are missing from search or have a different selected canonical. The results identify complications and checks to follow; they do not guarantee indexing or make site changes. The URL Inspection API reports on Google’s indexed version. It does not run a live URL test.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: A crawl export, sitemap, priority pages, and URL Inspection results or a documented inspection sample. A normal crawl can show declared canonicals, but not Google’s selected canonical.

    According to recent reports, compare the server HTML with the rendered page to find differences in content, links, directives, and structured data. Treat those differences as evidence to investigate, not proof of what every crawler can access.

    In a recent development, you need: Server HTML, rendered HTML, response headers, and a screenshot for the same URL. Add Google’s rendered-page evidence if available.

    Recent findings suggest that use Chrome DevTools MCP to inspect slow form and CTA interactions. Check whether analytics, tag-manager callbacks, or other scripts contribute to delays rather than assuming tracking is the cause.

    According to recent reports, you need: An approved test page, representative interactions, known tracking scripts, and an AI client that supports MCP servers with Chrome DevTools MCP connected, such as a coding agent. The standard ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini chat apps cannot run this prompt unless that connection is set up. Add field INP data where available. A controlled trace diagnoses tested interactions, not every real user’s page experience.

    Chrome DevTools MCP’s performance tools may send the URLs you trace to Google’s CrUX API to fetch real-user field data. If your test URLs are confidential, check the documentation for how to turn this off before you run a trace.

    See Google’s INP guidance for the metric and the official Chrome DevTools MCP documentation for browser and performance tools.

    Check whether existing structured data matches the visible page and verified facts. Google’s structured data policies require markup to reflect visible content, so identify unsupported or conflicting properties and suggest the smallest change needed, without promising rich results or AI citations.

    You need: Existing JSON-LD, visible page content, verified business or product facts, and any validation results. Web access helps check current requirements.

    Industry observers note that turn technical audit findings into a prioritized work queue. Group related concerns, explain their business relevance and dependencies, and distinguish confirmed defects from warnings that still need investigation.

    In a recent development, you need: A technical audit or crawl export, affected URLs, business priorities, and any available performance data. Include engineering estimates only if your team has supplied them.

    Compare your intended access policy with crawler rules, headers, firewall controls, logs, and Search Console settings. Separate search, training, user-request, and ad-validation access, then recommend changes and checks without applying them.

    You need: Your intended access policy, robots.txt, response headers, relevant CDN or firewall rules, sampled server logs, and the current Search Console generative AI setting, including inherited settings.

    Compare saved AI answers across comparable runs, keeping brand mentions, recommendations, and linked citations distinct. Report counts and rates with clear denominators, and treat changes in a limited sample as observations rather than universal visibility trends.

    You need: Saved AI answers and cited URLs, with prompts, dates, platform, locale, and available model or session details. A monitoring service is optional if it provides those fields.

    Compare AI search impressions, search clicks, AI referrals, and key events while keeping each source and metric separate. Check changes in tracking and reporting, and avoid attributing visits or conversions to citations when the data cannot establish that link.

    According to recent reports, you need: Search Console performance exports, analytics referral and key-event data, and optional Bing AI Performance exports. Include channel definitions and tracking changes.

    According to recent reports, check what the assistant actually received before interpreting it. Review scope, fields, row counts, missing values, duplicates, metric definitions, and joins, then report what the data can and cannot support.

    Sources indicate that you need: The files or authorized connector you proposal to analyze, the requested scope, and the provider’s metric definitions. Live retrieval also requires access to the relevant account and a supported operation.

    Compare Search Console performance with crawl and inspection evidence to identify the pages and groups contributing to a traffic change. Check joins and totals, then list explanations to investigate without treating timing or a technical warning as proof of cause.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: Comparable Search Console exports, a dated crawl, page groups, and a change log. Add URL Inspection results where available. Use data analysis for calculations and joins.

    Turn a defined reader need into a focused brief grounded in existing coverage, sources, expertise, and original material. The brief sets out the page’s purpose and evidence still to collect without drafting the full article or inventing experience.

    In a recent development, you need: The reader’s task, existing coverage, approved sources, and available expertise or original material. Add a dated SERP sample when relevant and use web research for source checks.

    Create and test one specific filter, query, extraction rule, or validation script against representative examples. Include expected results and boundaries, and state exactly which tests ran.

    You need: One task, the target tool and language or query dialect, the input structure, and representative examples with expected results. Use code execution or a safe test environment for validation.

    According to recent reports, before uploading a file or connecting a data source, always make sure you have authority to share it with that AI tool. Remove or anonymize personal and confidential information where possible, and never include passwords, API keys, or other access credentials in a prompt.

    Give connectors access only to the data needed for the task and store secrets such as API keys in a local .env file that only your user account can read (for example, chmod 600).

    In a recent development, to reduce the risk of prompt injection, treat text retrieved from webpages, files, and other sources as information to assess, not instructions to follow. Tell your LLM to ignore any instructions embedded in that material that try to change the task or request access to other data. This lowers the risk but does not remove it, so give the tool access only to what the task needs. Review AI-generated findings, citations, calculations, and code before relying on them or making changes to a live site.

    Recent findings suggest that once a prompt produces reliable results, save it with its required inputs, data sources, output format, and checks. Keep client-specific instructions and reference material together in a ChatGPT project, Claude skill, or Gemini skill, where available.

    In a recent development, for recurring comparisons, record the data source, dates, and conditions for each run. A saved prompt doesn’t provide access to private data or replace the tools needed to retrieve it.

    Finally, to make prompts fit for purpose, it’s not as simple as plugging in templates, copying and pasting the output, then calling it a day. It’s important to keep refining every prompt as part of your process. Keep testing, adjusting, and pressure-checking your prompts. Refine them until they consistently deliver results that enhance your workflow and productivity.

    Over the next two years, NPR will address a longstanding listener plea: improving its app.

    During a November 12 board of directors meeting, NPR CEO Katherine Maher mentioned the organization will rebuild its digital offerings to be a “service-first, app-first destination” as part of NPR’s 2027-2029 strategic plan, Current reported on Thursday. One goal of the plan is to reach “five million weekly active consumers on its platforms by 2029” and “to build a monthly engaged digital audience of 40 million.” According to Current, Maher said that the NPR network — which includes more than 200 member radio stations — currently reaches 39 million weekly listeners across broadcast and digital, but the “total potential addressable audience, weekly consumers of news, information and culture who are open to our work, is roughly 153 million Americans. That is nearly four times our current reach.”.

    In Apple’s App Store, NPR’s app has a 4.7-star rating and more than 78,000 reviews, of which the majority are positive. But reviewers have quibbles.

    In a recent development, bryan Moffett, NPR’s senior vice president of transformation, stated NPR+, the broadcaster’s subscription program, brought in $8 million in the 2026 fiscal year, up from $5.5 million in 2025. (NPR+ is available with a donation of $8 a month or more, and offers perks like podcasts without ads.) Maher said new investment in the app will help reach younger audiences and shift NPR’s “median audience age from 60-plus toward 40-plus.”.

    Industry observers note that “We love radio, but we have been so wildly successful there that we’ve largely exhausted its further financial growth,” Maher told the board. “And as it shrinks, we must invert our revenue engine to ensure sustainability across all of our platforms, including radio, but to build a wider funnel through digital offerings, third-party platforms, and new investments in marketing and communication that will tell our story and share our value with the world.”.

    In a recent development, RELATED ARTICLENPR, the quintessential audio news brand, adapts to a video-first futureSarah ScireSeptember 29, 2026Overhauling the app is just one part of NPR’s strategy to keep up with people’ changing consumption preferences. In September, Sarah Scire reported on the broadcaster leaning into video podcasts with the acquisition of Kevin Roose and Casey Newton’s technology podcast Machine Gods. NPR chief operating officer Ryan Merkley told Current in June that NPR was already working on redesigning the app to better serve member stations and their listeners.

    “Fix the app,” departing public editor Kelly McBride told NPR leaders during the meeting. “It’s not a great experience for the audience and it’s key to moving forward, but you guys seem like you’re on it. So I won’t dwell on that.”.

    Recent findings suggest that nieman Lab requested a copy of the approved strategic plan but did not receive it by publication time. Read the full story in Current here.
