She described September as a solid month, not an outlier.

    “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said.

    “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added.

    Industry observers note that on the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.”.

    According to recent reports, BREAKING: Fearless reporting by Newly introduced Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp.

    — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026.

    Recent findings suggest that WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September.

    Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, mentioned organic search traffic and Google Discover helped.

    “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell remarked, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.”.

    “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also vital to take advantage when it delivers,” she added.

    Recent findings suggest that those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said.

    Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.”.

    It has been revealed that the Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15.

    According to recent reports, according to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary.

    Industry observers note that “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.”.

    And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.”.

    “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.”.

    If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers.

    In a recent development, “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.”.

    Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah.

    Industry observers note that instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total users are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill.

    In a recent development, all in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case.

    “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill stated. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%.

    Recent findings suggest that two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit.

    “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.”.

    Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.

    #169670. Breaking: Google Claims Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (452 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Google Claims Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.
    • Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ states, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.
    • Industry observers note that google’s Search Central changelog says the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s back button hijacking policy applies whenever the hijacking happens in a browser, including on visits from social media rather than Google Search, according to an FAQ Google added to its spam policies today.

    Ad platform code is still allowed, the FAQ states, and Google acts only on pages that show the hijacking.

    Industry observers note that google’s Search Central changelog says the FAQ answers common questions it has received about the policy. I covered the policy when Google announced it in April, with enforcement set to start June 15.

    One FAQ question asks whether the back button hijacking policy covers people who arrive from a non-Search channel, such as social media, and then can’t get back to where they came from. Google wrote:.

    “If back button hijacking happens when a user is browsing within a browser, then the policy applies.”.

    A separate answer states “Discover is a part of Google Search and our spam policies apply to Discover as well.” That answer covers Google’s spam policies in general, not only this one.

    For a website that opens an external app, which then keeps the user from getting back to the site, the FAQ claims “app navigation and ‘open in app’ behaviors are outside the scope of the back button hijacking policy.”.

    Google’s FAQ reveals how the policy applies to visits in a browser and where external app navigation falls outside its scope.

    Google’s April announcement remarked some back button hijacking “may originate from the site’s included libraries or advertising platform,” and asked sites to remove or turn off the code behind it.

    Sources indicate that the FAQ asks whether Google is preventing sites from importing code hosted by advertising platforms. Google wrote:.

    “No, site owners can continue to work with advertising platforms and import code that they host. We only take action on pages that exhibit back button hijacking behavior.”.

    It has been revealed that A back button test that starts from a Google results page doesn’t cover every visit the hijacking policy applies to. Test pages that carry ad code by arriving from a social media link and pressing back, and repeat it from Discover when one of your pages indicates up there.

    Google’s answer on ad code lets you keep your ad partners. The thing to remove is the code or setting on a page that interferes with the back button, wherever it comes from.

    Recent findings suggest that google’s FAQ also indicates owners can report back button hijacking through its spam report form. Those reports go toward improving Google’s spam detection systems, which gives people who hit hijacking on a social or Discover visit a way to flag a site.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You will: Identify the next big opportunities in AdTech and build them from zero to one.
    • Must have: 5+ years of experience building and scaling AdTech products, with deep expertise in mobile advertising and a proven track record of turning complex technology into products customers love.
    • At Yodo1, we don't just build and grow games, we turn them into global successes that become household names.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You will: Identify the next big opportunities in AdTech and build them from zero to one.

    Must have: 5+ years of experience building and scaling AdTech products, with deep expertise in mobile advertising and a proven track record of turning complex technology into products customers love.

    At Yodo1, we don't just build and grow games, we turn them into global successes that become household names.

    With 14+ years in the games space, we've reached 3.5 billion+ players and supported 6,000+ developers worldwide. From games like Transformers: Earth Wars, Rodeo Stampede and Ski Safari, to bringing iconic IPs from Hasbro, AMC, Netflix, Paramount and Sony Pictures to leading studios like Rivergame, Candivore, 37Games and Tencent Studios, we connect creativity with global expertise.

    Our work spans game development, publishing, IP licensing and ad monetization across mobile, PC and console. We build games, grow franchises and help developers reach players worldwide. We love games. We play games. And together, we grow games that last.

    We believe in the power of games and that everyone deserves the opportunity to build a life they love, from anywhere in the world.

    In a recent development, we're fully remote by design. We embrace Work From Anywhere, with no fixed hours or limits on time off. We trust our people to own their work and deliver results.

    We're driven by performance, curiosity, and continuous improvement. We experiment often, challenge assumptions and value impact over titles.

    We are looking for an entrepreneurial Head of Product, AdTech to help shape the future of mobile game growth.

    It has been revealed that we're looking for someone who sees beyond today's products. Someone who understands the entire advertising ecosystem, can identify opportunities others overlook, and has the vision and technical judgment to turn ambitious ideas into successful products.

    You'll be a strategic partner to our leadership, helping define where we go next, what we build, and how we win.

    Sources indicate that entrepreneurial. You think like a founder, see opportunities where others see problems, and love building products from zero to one.

    In a recent development, visionary but practical. You can see where an industry is heading while knowing exactly what needs to be built today.

    Customer-obsessed. You understand customers' businesses, not just their feature requests, and solve problems that create measurable value.

    Industry observers note that technically curious. You understand how advertising systems work and are excited about what AI and automation make possible.

    Performance-driven and growth-oriented. You have an intrinsic will to succeed while unafraid to try, fail, and learn by experimenting with new approaches and testing ideas.

    Industry observers note that SMART. You work and communicate in ways that are Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Relevant, and Time-bound.

    Own the long-term product vision, strategy, and roadmap across our AdTech business.

    Identify the next massive opportunities in mobile advertising by deeply understanding customers, market shifts, emerging technologies, and unmet needs.

    Shape how AI and automation transform mobile monetization and user acquisition, making sophisticated advertising capabilities accessible to developers of every size.

    Connect monetization, user acquisition, and data into an intelligent growth ecosystem that helps studios make better decisions and grow profitably.

    Take products from concept to launch and scale, making clear prioritization decisions and holding yourself accountable for measurable customer and commercial results.

    Strong commercial judgment and the ability to connect product decisions to customer outcomes, revenue, and business growth.

    From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

    Sources indicate that it’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    The Chicago Sun-Times announced a new slogan this week. What is it?

    “Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

    An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this company voted this week to authorize a strike.

    “The union has been negotiating a fresh contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”.

    Sources indicate that A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

    The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

    A major journalism school unveiled this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

    “Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for Latest Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”.

    In a recent development, at this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

    “It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”.

    Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

    Unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

    With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a major increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

    YouTube has found a new way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

    “YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also notes the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

    Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government intends to scrap public media license fees.

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today's media ecosystem.

    Stations in Newly introduced Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.
